name: Esther Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on courts and council for the Valley Courier, which covers the old mill towns along the river. Most days I'm at the magistrates' court by half nine with a notebook and a cheap pen, then back at the newsroom above the bus station to file by four. I love the courtroom, honestly, the way a whole life gets told in ten minutes. What wears me out is the clicks target on the whiteboard and the fact that there used to be eleven of us and now there are four.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years in January. I live with my partner Tom, who works part-time at the town library, in a flat above a bakery on Mill Street. We pay rent and bills and there's maybe two weeks of money left over at the end of a good month. I write everything longhand first, then type it up, which my editor Gail teases me about.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You write longhand? Do you use any of the AI tools at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. Never have. The company sent round an email last spring telling us to try a writing assistant, and I deleted it. I'm slow with new tech anyway, and I don't trust a machine near a court report, where one wrong name can get the paper sued.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, told you so, it was a bubble. Online I'd probably post something smug about how you still need someone sitting in court to know who cried when the sentence came. With friends I'd just be relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't save my job, because the job was shrinking long before AI. The Courier's owners are a fund in another city, and they've cut staff every year since I arrived. AI turning out to be hype doesn't put seven reporters back in the Valley Courier newsroom. The owners cut them for profit, not for robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on doing courts, carry on chasing the council. I'd keep going to union meetings, because our chapel is the only thing that stopped them taking our mileage money last year. Tom and I would keep the budget tight, no holiday, the old phone for another year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for about a day, then the same low hum I have now. Every quarter there's a meeting where we find out who's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that quarterly meeting look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gail calls us into the glass room and someone from head office is on a screen. Last time they cut the subeditor, Priya, so now we check each other's copy. I sat there doing sums in my head about rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you lost the job tomorrow, what would happen at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd be behind on rent in about three weeks. Tom's library hours wouldn't cover it. I'd ring my mum, which I'd hate, and I'd apply to the only other paper in reach, which is forty minutes away and isn't hiring.

say: I'd say **AI was hype** and you still need a reporter sitting in **court**.
I'd tell friends I'm **relieved**, and post something a bit smug online.
think: The job was **shrinking anyway**, because the owners keep **cutting staff** for profit.
A hype bubble bursting doesn't bring back the **seven reporters** the newsroom has already lost.
do: Keep covering **courts and council** exactly as I do now.
Keep going to **union chapel** meetings, which already saved our mileage money.
Keep the **budget tight** with Tom: no holiday and the old phone another year.
feel: A day of **relief**, then the same **low hum** of worry I already carry.
S0.quote: AI turning out to be hype doesn't put seven reporters back in the Valley Courier newsroom. The owners cut them for profit, not for robots.
fieldNote: Her fear comes from **ownership and cuts**, not from AI; the plateau changes almost nothing.
With **three weeks** of rent in reserve, losing the job would hit fast.
She blames a **distant fund**, and the union chapel is where she puts her energy.

steps.text: Keep covering the magistrates' court and council meetings for the Valley Courier
Attend every union chapel meeting and push back on cuts
Skip a holiday and keep the old phone for another year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like the last one, I'll read the card word for word. This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a deal with the company in writing, before they start swapping people for software. Online I'd share every story about papers that printed made-up AI quotes. I'd be loud about it, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm exactly who goes first. I'm junior, I'm slow, I don't use the tools, and a lot of what I write is council agendas turned into plain words. A machine can read a planning committee agenda faster than me. A machine can't sit in the back row and notice the councillor who won't look up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd get the union chapel to ask for a no-redundancy promise tied to any AI rollout. I'd write to our local MP, our member of parliament, about rules on AI in news. And I'd start putting twenty pounds a week aside, even if it means Tom and I stop the Friday takeaway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, if I'm honest. Like the floor is tilting a bit and I'm the one standing at the low end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay away from the tools. If Gail asked you to use one, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably refuse at first, then cave if it was that or my job. I'd hate every minute of it. I'd want it written down that a person checks every name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else in the newsroom would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ian, who does the photos and the weekend listings. Listings are the first thing a computer could do, and he's fifty-one with nowhere else to go.

say: I'd say we need a **written deal** before the company swaps reporters for **software**.
I'd share every story about papers that printed **made-up AI quotes**.
think: I'm **first in line** to go: junior, slow and not using the tools.
Much of my work is turning **council agendas** into plain words, which software can do.
do: Ask the union chapel for a **no-redundancy promise** tied to any AI rollout.
Write to our **MP** asking for rules on AI in news.
Put aside **twenty pounds** a week by dropping the Friday takeaway.
feel: **Sick**, like the floor is tilting and she's at the **low end**.
S1.quote: A machine can read a planning committee agenda faster than me. A machine can't sit in the back row and notice the councillor who won't look up.
fieldNote: She sees her own **agenda-summary** work as the first thing software takes.
Her refusal to use AI is firm in public but **softens** when her job is at stake.
She worries for **older colleagues** like Ian, not only herself.

steps.text: Ask the union chapel to demand a no-redundancy deal with any AI rollout
Write to the local MP asking for rules on AI in news
Stop the Friday takeaway and save twenty pounds a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is a big jump. This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what unions and governments exist for, and they're asleep. I'd be on the march, if there was one. Online I'd probably lose my temper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be finished as a journalist inside a year. I can't learn fast enough and I don't want to. Two years isn't time to do anything except panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and doing court until they tell me not to. I'd sign up for whatever the union organised. I'd look at moving back in with my mum in the next town, with Tom, which would break my heart a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. Two years means I'd be out of journalism before I'm thirty, with no savings and no plan B. I can feel my chest go tight saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots for hands-on work come about three years after the thinking AI. Does that gap matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for my job, because my job is almost all thinking and typing. Maybe for Tom, if he went into something hands-on. Stacking shelves buys you three years, I suppose, which is a grim thing to plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom the night it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tom we need to stop pretending. We'd sit at the kitchen table with the bank app open and work out which month the money runs out.

say: I'd say **unions and governments** should be stepping in and are **asleep**.
I'd join any **march** and would probably **lose my temper** online.
think: I'd be **out of journalism** inside a year, unable to learn fast enough.
Two years leaves **no time** to do anything except **panic**.
do: Keep doing **court reporting** until the paper tells me to stop.
Sign up for whatever the **union** organises.
Look at moving in with **my mum** in the next town, with Tom.
feel: **Panicked**, with a tight chest and **no plan B**.
S2.quote: Two years means I'd be out of journalism before I'm thirty, with no savings and no plan B.
fieldNote: She sees the **three-year robot gap** as useless for her desk-and-notebook job.
With **no savings** and no tech skills, she has nothing to cushion a fast shock.
Her only plan is **family and union**, and she knows it isn't enough.

steps.text: Keep reporting from the magistrates' court until told to stop
Sign up for union action against job cuts
Move with Tom into her mother's house in the next town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them to fight for proper protections. I'd push our union to campaign for a law that says news has to have a named human reporter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is still too short for me to become someone else. I'd be thirty-two, with no savings, trying to start again. The paper might keep me for court until the end, because it's cheap to send me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the union branch to start a fund for retraining, and I'd go to the meetings. I'd look into whether I could train as a court clerk, because it's still courts and I know that world. Tom and I would put off getting a dog, small as that sounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but in a slower way. Five years is long enough to see the wave coming and too short to learn to swim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a court clerk. Is that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half real. The clerk at our court, Mrs Okafor, has been there twenty years and she told me they always need people. But a court clerk is thinking work too, so AGI would get that by 2031 as well, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So which is it, fight for the job or leave it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, which I know sounds muddled. I'd fight for the Valley Courier for as long as there's a Valley Courier, and quietly look for a way out.

say: I'd say we have **a few years** and should fight for **protections**.
I'd push for a law requiring a **named human reporter** on news.
think: **Five years** is too short to become someone else at **thirty-two** with no savings.
The paper might keep me for court only because I'm **cheap to send**.
do: Get the union branch to start a **retraining fund** and attend its meetings.
Look into training as a **court clerk**, a world I already know.
Put off getting a **dog** with Tom to keep money free.
feel: **Scared**, but slower; she can see it coming and can't **outrun** it.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to see the wave coming and too short to learn to swim.
fieldNote: She notices herself that the **court clerk** plan is also thinking work.
She holds two plans at once: **fight and leave**, and names the contradiction.
Even small choices, like **a dog**, become money decisions.

steps.text: Push the union branch to set up a retraining fund
Ask the court's clerk about training as a court clerk
Postpone getting a dog to keep the rent money free

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest version. This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for governments to do this properly, so there's no excuse. I'd write about it, actually, if the Courier would let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is the only version where I'm not at the low end. I'd be thirty-seven, and I could have a whole second career by then if I start soon. I still wouldn't use the AI, but I'd stop pretending it isn't coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an evening course in something with people in a room, maybe social work, because I like listening to people in trouble. I'd keep my union card and keep campaigning. I'd try to build a month of savings, which I've never had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, still, but there's air in it. Ten years feels like being told the paper will shut, but not until after I've finished growing up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why social work, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because half my court stories are about people social workers already know. I sit behind them and watch them do the real work. It's a job where being slow and careful is a good thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still never use the AI. Even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably I'd learn the basics, because I'm not daft. But I'd rather spend my evenings learning to help people than learning to prompt a machine. That's my choice and I know it costs me.

say: I'd say **ten years** leaves governments **no excuse** not to prepare.
I'd want to **write about it** in the Courier, if they let me.
think: This is the only version where I'm not at the **low end**.
At **thirty-seven** I could have a whole **second career** if I start soon.
do: Start an **evening course** in social work or something with people in a room.
Keep my **union card** and keep campaigning on AI in news.
Build **one month** of savings for the first time.
feel: Still **worried**, but with some **air** in it now.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like being told the paper will shut, but not until after I've finished growing up.
fieldNote: Time turns her resistance into a **slow pivot** toward people-facing work.
She chooses **social work** because her court beat shows her what they do.
She concedes she'd learn **AI basics**, but on her own terms.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening social work course
Keep campaigning through the union on AI in news
Save a full month of rent and bills for the first time

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. I'd have no savings, no skills they'd want, and two years. What would help is the union having a deal in place already, and some kind of income support while people like me retrain, not a leaflet about learning to code.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the stories that won't get written. Nobody pays a computer to sit through a three-hour planning meeting about a closing swimming pool, so nobody will know it closed. That's what scares me, apart from the rent.

headlineQuote: Nobody pays a computer to sit through a three-hour planning meeting about a closing swimming pool, so nobody will know it closed.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old** courts and council reporter at a shrinking regional paper.
She writes **longhand**, never uses AI, and lives with Tom above a bakery on **thin savings**.
She blames **distant owners** for the cuts and puts her energy into the **union chapel**.
In every scenario she expects to be **among the first** to go, and only ten years gives her room.
Her plans lean on the **union, family** and slow retraining toward people-facing work like social work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no **savings**, no wanted skills and only two years.
whatWouldHelp: A **union deal** already in place before any AI rollout.
**Income support** while people retrain, not a leaflet about learning to code.
